newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech minister says crown devaluation unnecessary.
newsitem.headline: Czech minister says crown devaluation unnecessary.

text.p: A devaluation of the Czech crown is not needed although the current account deficit, at $3.1 billion in the first three quarters, is hardly bearable, a senior minister was quoted as saying on Friday.
"It really is not necessary to change the exchange rate," the leftwing daily Rude Pravo quoted Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy as telling parliament's foreign affairs committee.
But he added that a responsible official would not admit to planning such a move even the night before doing it.

The newspaper reported him as saying that the current account deficit was on the verge of not being bearable, but no direct quote was provided. Dlouhy and officials at his ministry were not immediately available for further comment on Friday.
Czech National Bank Governor Josef Tosovsky said last week that the full-year current account deficit could reach seven percent of gross domestic product (GDP), up from four percent last year.
The deficit comes from a record 112 billion crown merchandise trade deficit for the first nine months.
But in repeating his position that a devaluation of the crown is not necessary, Tosovsky said the deficit could be financed and posed no danger in the medium-term.
The capital account had a roughly $2 billion surplus through the first three months of 1996.
Dlouhy told the committee that each economy had its own level of tolerance for a current account deficit without posing a threat to economic stability, Pravo reported.
It said Dlouhy sees the deficit, and specifically the foreign trade gap, as "the most critical parametres of otherwise solid macroeconomic situation in the Czech Republic".
The current account showed a $580 million deficit in the first nine months of 1995, but a surge in imports has been welcomed as needed for modernising Czech industry.
Both Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus and Tosovsky have repeatedly ruled out a crown devalutation.
Klaus said recently that the country would have a perpetual merchandise trade deficit due to the structure of its economy and lack of natural resources.
